Abstract.

We establish a tantalizing symmetry of certain numbers refining the Narayana numbers. In terms of Dyck paths, this symmetry is interpreted in the following way: if wn,k,mw_{n,k,m} is the number of Dyck paths of semilength nn with kk occurrences of U​DUD and mm occurrences of U​U​DUUD, then w2​k+1,k,m=w2​k+1,k,k+1−mw_{2k+1,k,m}=w_{2k+1,k,k+1-m}. We give a combinatorial proof of this fact, relying on the cycle lemma, and showing that the numbers w2​k+1,k,mw_{2k+1,k,m} are multiples of the Narayana numbers. We prove a more general fact establishing a relationship between the numbers wn,k,mw_{n,k,m} and a family of generalized Narayana numbers due to Callan. A closed-form expression for the even more general numbers wn,k1,k2,…,krw_{n,k_{1},k_{2},\ldots,k_{r}} counting the semilength-nn Dyck paths with k1k_{1} U​DUD-factors, k2k_{2} U​U​DUUD-factors, …\ldots , and krk_{r} Ur​DU^{r}D-factors is also obtained, as well as a more general form of the discussed symmetry for these numbers in the case when all rise runs are of certain minimal length. Finally, we investigate properties of the polynomials Wn,k​(t)=∑m=0kwn,k,m​tmW_{n,k}(t)=\sum_{m=0}^{k}w_{n,k,m}t^{m}, including real-rootedness, γ\gamma-positivity, and a symmetric decomposition.

1. Introduction

A lattice path is a path in the discrete integer lattice ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} consisting of a sequence of steps from a prescribed step set and satisfying prescribed restrictions. Among classical lattice paths, Dyck paths are perhaps the most well-studied. A Dyck path of semilength nn is a path in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} with step set S={(1,1),(1,−1)}S=\{(1,1),(1,-1)\} that starts at the origin (0,0)(0,0), ends at (2​n,0)(2n,0), and never traverses below the horizontal axis. The steps (1,1)(1,1) are called up steps and can be represented by the letter UU, while the steps (1,−1)(1,-1) are down steps and denoted DD. It is well known that the number of Dyck paths of semilength nn is the Catalan number Cn=OPEN(2​nnCLOSE)/(n+1)C_{n}=\binom{2n}{n}/(n+1) which is known to enumerate more than 250 other families of combinatorial objects [27].

The number of Dyck paths of semilength nn that contain exactly kk places where a UU is immediately followed by a DD—called U​DUD-factors (or peaks)—is equal to the Narayana number Nn,kN_{n,k} defined by

Nn,k=1n​OPEN(nkCLOSE)​OPEN(nk−1CLOSE),N_{n,k}=\frac{1}{n}\binom{n}{k}\binom{n}{k-1},

for all 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n and N0,0=1N_{0,0}=1. Knowing this, it is easy to see that Nn,kN_{n,k} also counts the number of Dyck paths of semilength nn with k−1k-1 D​UDU-factors (valleys). The Narayana numbers are known to exhibit the symmetry Nn,k=Nn,n+1−kN_{n,k}=N_{n,n+1-k}, which can be proved combinatorially via several involutions; see, for example, [12, 18, 19, 20].

There is interest in counting Dyck paths (and other kinds of lattice paths) by the number of occurrences of longer factors, or even finding the joint distribution of occurrences of multiple kinds of factors. Two early works in this direction are [11, 26]. In [29], Wang discusses a general technique that is useful for obtaining the relevant generating functions in many such cases; see also [30]. Our work is concerned with the joint distribution of U​DUD-factors and U​U​DUUD-factors over Dyck paths. This does not seem to have been studied before, and is different from the instances discussed in the works cited above as the factor U​DUD is an ending segment of the factor U​U​DUUD. We can also interpret these factors in terms of rise runs—maximal consecutive subsequences of up steps—as the number of U​DUD-factors is equal to the total number of rise runs, and the number of U​U​DUUD-factors is equal to the number of rise runs of length at least 2.

Let wn,k,mw_{n,k,m} be the number of Dyck paths of semilength nn with kk U​DUD-factors and mm U​U​DUUD-factors. Then we have the following symmetry:

Theorem 1.1.

For all 1≤m≤k1\leq m\leq k, we have

w2​k+1,k,m=w2​k+1,k,k+1−m.w_{2k+1,k,m}=w_{2k+1,k,k+1-m}.

In other words, among all Dyck paths of semilength 2​k+12k+1 with kk U​DUD-factors, the number of those with mm U​U​DUUD-factors is equal to the number of those with k+1−mk+1-m U​U​DUUD-factors. To prove this symmetry, the first and third authors used generating function techniques to derive the following closed formula for the numbers wn,k,mw_{n,k,m} (see Section 6 in the Appendix), from which Theorem 1.1 readily follows.

Theorem 1.2.

We have

wn,k,m={1k​OPEN(nk−1CLOSE)​OPEN(n−k−1m−1CLOSE)​OPEN(kmCLOSE), if 0<m≤k,and k+m≤n,1, if ​m=0​ and ​n=k,0, otherwise.w_{n,k,m}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle{\frac{1}{k}\binom{n}{k-1}\binom{n-k-1}{m-1}\binom{k}{m}},&\text{ if }0<m\leq k,\,\text{and }k+m\leq n,\\ 1,&\text{ if }m=0\text{ and }n=k,\\ 0,&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

Nonetheless, Theorem 1.1 cries for combinatorial explanation, but a combinatorial proof eluded the first and third authors for several years. The remaining authors joined this project in Summer 2022 as part of the AMS Mathematics Research Community Trees in Many Contexts, during which we found a combinatorial proof for Theorem 1.1. This proof is the main focus of the current paper. In fact, we give a combinatorial proof for the following identity relating the numbers w2​k+1,k,mw_{2k+1,k,m} to Narayana numbers.

Theorem 1.3.

For all k≥1k\geq 1 and m≥0m\geq 0, we have

(1.1) w2​k+1,k,m=OPEN(2​k+1k−1CLOSE)​Nk,m.w_{2k+1,k,m}=\binom{2k+1}{k-1}N_{k,m}.

Observe that Theorem 1.1 follows immediately from Theorem 1.3 and the symmetry of the Narayana numbers. Our combinatorial proof of Theorem 1.3 requires heavy use of the cycle lemma. We show that analogous statements to Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.3 hold for the numbers w2​k−1,k,mw_{2k-1,k,m}. We also generalize Theorem 1.3 to a relationship between the wn,k,mw_{n,k,m} and a family of generalized Narayana numbers introduced by Callan  [8] (see Theorem 4.2).

Using the ideas in the combinatorial proofs of Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.2, we establish the following more general statements for wn,k1,k2,…,krw_{n,k_{1},k_{2},\ldots,k_{r}}, defined to be the number of Dyck paths of semilength nn with k1k_{1} U​DUD-factors, k2k_{2} U​U​DUUD-factors, …, and krk_{r} Ur​DU^{r}D-factors.

Theorem 1.4.

For all r≥2r\geq 2 and 1≤m≤k1\leq m\leq k, taking k1=k2=…=kr−1=kk_{1}=k_{2}=\ldots=k_{r-1}=k, we have

wr​k+1,k,k,…,k,m=wr​k+1,k,k,…,k,k+1−mw_{rk+1,k,k,\ldots,k,m}=w_{rk+1,k,k,\ldots,k,k+1-m}

and

wr​k−1,k,k,…,k,m=wr​k−1,k,k,…,k,k−m.w_{rk-1,k,k,\ldots,k,m}=w_{rk-1,k,k,\ldots,k,k-m}.

Note that r=2r=2 recovers the symmetry of the numbers w2​k±1,k,mw_{2k\pm 1,k,m} (our Theorems 1.1 and 3.8). Observe also that in terms of rise runs, Theorem 1.4 describes a symmetry in the case when all rise runs in the considered Dyck paths are of length at least r−1r-1.

Theorem 1.5.

Let r≥1r\geq 1, k1≥k2≥⋯≥kr≥0k_{1}\geq k_{2}\geq\cdots\geq k_{r}\geq 0, and n≥k1+k2+⋯+krn\geq k_{1}+k_{2}+\cdots+k_{r}. Take k^=k1+k2+⋯+kr−1\hat{k}=k_{1}+k_{2}+\cdots+k_{r-1}. Then

wn,k1,k2,…,kr={1k1​OPEN(nk1−1CLOSE)​OPEN(n−k^−1kr−1CLOSE)​OPEN(k1k1−k2,k2−k3,…,kr−1−kr,krCLOSE), if ​kr>0,1k1​OPEN(nk1−1CLOSE)​OPEN(k1k1−k2,k2−k3,…,kr−1−kr,krCLOSE), if ​kr=0​ and ​n=k^,0, otherwise.w_{n,k_{1},k_{2},\ldots,k_{r}}=\\ \begin{cases}\displaystyle{\frac{1}{k_{1}}\binom{n}{k_{1}-1}\binom{n-\hat{k}-1}{k_{r}-1}\binom{k_{1}}{k_{1}-k_{2},k_{2}-k_{3},\ldots,k_{r-1}-k_{r},k_{r}}},&\text{ if }k_{r}>0,\\[10.03749pt] \displaystyle{\frac{1}{k_{1}}\binom{n}{k_{1}-1}\binom{k_{1}}{k_{1}-k_{2},k_{2}-k_{3},\ldots,k_{r-1}-k_{r},k_{r}}},&\text{ if }k_{r}=0\text{ and }n=\hat{k},\\[2.00749pt] 0,&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

Theorem 1.5 specializes to the formula for Narayana numbers upon setting r=1r=1 and to Theorem 1.2 for r=2r=2.

We note that the numbers wn,k,mw_{n,k,m} have been independently studied under different guises in the Ph.D. theses of Wang and Lemus-Vidales. Wang [29, Theorem 2] gave a formula for the joint distribution of U​UUU-factors and U​U​DUUD-factors over Dyck paths of semilength nn. Wang’s formula is equivalent to our formula in Theorem 1.2, as a Dyck path of semilength nn with kk occurrences of U​DUD has n−kn-k occurrences of U​UUU. Moreover, Lemus-Vidales [21, Theorem 3.1.3] gave an analogous formula for counting Dyck paths by “short peaks” (i.e., U​DUD-factors not preceded by a UU), U​U​UUUU-factors, and U​U​DUUD-factors. It is shown in [21, Lemma 3.1.1] that the number of U​DUD-factors of a Dyck path is the sum of its number of short peaks and U​U​DUUD-factors and that the semilength is equal to the sum of its number of short peaks, U​U​UUUU-factors, and twice its number of U​U​DUUD-factors. Hence, Theorem 1.2 can be recovered from Lemus-Vidales’s formula. Though Wang and Lemus-Vidales’ results provide alternate routes to obtain some of our results, their formulas are obtained by deriving an appropriate functional equation and applying Lagrange inversion; neither of them had a combinatorial proof. One more relevant and recent result is by Fu and Yang [17], who found that wn,k,mw_{n,k,m} also counts plane trees with nn edges, kk internal nodes, and mm internal nodes with degree larger than one.

2. Preliminaries

Here, we introduce the background material necessary for the forthcoming combinatorial proofs.

2.1. Dyck paths

Recall that a Dyck path of semilength nn is a path in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} that begins at the origin, ends at (2​n,0)(2n,0), never goes below the horizontal axis, and consists of a sequence of up steps (1,1)(1,1) and down steps (1,−1)(1,-1). We can represent Dyck paths as Dyck words: words π\pi on the alphabet {U,D}\{U,D\} with the same number of UU’s and DD’s, such that there are never more DD’s than UU’s in any prefix of π\pi. When we refer to a U​DUD- or U​U​DUUD-factor in a Dyck path, we really mean a factor in the corresponding Dyck word.

2.2. Cyclic compositions and the cycle lemma

Given a sequence p=p1p2⋯pnp=p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{n}, we say that a sequence p′p^{\prime} is a cyclic shift (or cyclic rotation) of pp if p′p^{\prime} is of the form

p′=pipi+1⋯pnp1p2⋯pi−1,p^{\prime}=p_{i}p_{i+1}\cdots p_{n}p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i-1},

for some 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. Let us write p∼p′p\sim p^{\prime} whenever pp and p′p^{\prime} are cyclic shifts of each other.

Let 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k\mathsf{Comp}_{n,k} denote the set of all compositions of nn into kk parts, i.e., a sequence of kk positive integers whose sum is nn. We define a cyclic composition [μ][\mu] to be the equivalence class of a composition μ\mu under cyclic shift. Let 𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k\mathsf{CComp}_{n,k} be the set of cyclic compositions consisting of compositions of nn into kk parts, which is well-defined because the number of parts of a composition and the sum of its parts are clearly invariant under cyclic shift. We define the order of a cyclic composition [μ][\mu], denoted by 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]\mathsf{ord}[\mu], to be the number of representatives of [μ][\mu]—that is, the number of distinct compositions that can be obtained from cyclically shifting μ\mu. Note that applying 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]\mathsf{ord}[\mu] cyclic shifts to μ\mu will return back μ\mu. If [μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n,k} has order kk, then we say that [μ][\mu] is primitive.

For any [μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n,k}, there exists a positive integer dd dividing both nn and kk such that [μ][\mu] is a concatenation of dd copies of a primitive cyclic composition [ν]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n/d,k/d[\nu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n/d,k/d}, which means that there exists ν¯∈[ν]\bar{\nu}\in[\nu] for which μ\mu is a concatenation of dd copies of ν¯\bar{\nu}. In this case, 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]=k/d=𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[ν]\mathsf{ord}[\mu]=k/d=\mathsf{ord}[\nu]. (If d=1d=1, then [μ][\mu] itself is primitive and is a concatenation of itself.) For example, the cyclic composition [1,2,1,1,2,1][1,2,1,1,2,1] is a concatenation of two copies of the primitive cyclic composition [1,2,1][1,2,1], and both of these cyclic compositions have order 3. Observe that this decomposition of cyclic compositions into primitive cyclic compositions is unique.

Lemma 2.1.

If nn and kk are relatively prime, then [μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n,k} is primitive.

Proof.

Let [μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n,k}. Then [μ][\mu] can be uniquely decomposed as a concatenation of dd copies of a primitive cyclic composition, where dd is a common divisor of nn and kk. Since nn and kk are relatively prime, it follows that d=1d=1, whence it follows that [μ][\mu] itself is primitive. ∎

The cycle lemma will play an important role in our proofs. Given a positive integer kk and a sequence p=p1p2⋯plp=p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{l} consisting only of UU’s and DD’s, we say that pp is kk-dominating if every prefix of pp (i.e., every sequence p1p2⋯pip_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{i} where 1≤i≤l1\leq i\leq l) has more copies of UU than kk times the number of copies of DD.

Lemma 2.2 (Cycle lemma [15]).

Let kk be a positive integer. For any sequence p=p1p2⋯pm+np=p_{1}p_{2}\cdots p_{m+n} consisting of mm copies of UU and nn copies of DD, there are exactly max​(0,m−k​n)\text{max}(0,m-kn) cyclic shifts of pp that are kk-dominating.

We refer to [10, 15] for a proof of the cycle lemma as well as some applications. We note that Raney [25] showed that the cycle lemma is equivalent to the Lagrange inversion formula; Raney’s proof was later generalized to the multivariate case by Bacher and Schaeffer [2].

Corollary 2.3 (of the cycle lemma).

Any sequence of kk copies of ○\bigcirc and k+1k+1 copies of □\square has exactly one cyclic shift with no proper prefix having more □\squares than ○\bigcircs.

Proof.

Given any sequence λ\lambda of kk copies of ○\bigcirc and k+1k+1 copies of □\square, let λ~\tilde{\lambda} be the reverse sequence of λ\lambda—that is, the sequence consisting of the entries of λ\lambda but in reverse order. The cycle lemma guarantees that there is exactly one cyclic shift of λ~\tilde{\lambda} that is 11-dominating. The reverse sequence of this 11-dominating cyclic shift is the cyclic shift of λ\lambda that has no proper prefix having more □\squares than ○\bigcircs. ∎

3. Combinatorial proof of formulas for wn,k,mw_{n,k,m}

3.1. Combinatorial proof of Theorem  1.2

We will give a combinatorial proof for the explicit formula of the numbers wn,k,mw_{n,k,m} stated in Theorem 1.2. This proof will require the notion of “extended peaks” and the decomposition of a Dyck word into “extended peaks”.

Definition 3.1.

An extended peak is a word in the alphabet {U,D}\{U,D\} consisting of a nonempty sequence of UU’s followed by one DD. Given an extended peak S=Ua​DS=U^{a}D, define its up-length, denoted by ℓ⁡(S)\ell(S), as ℓ⁡(S)≔a\ell(S)\coloneqq a.

We define a necklace of extended peaks (or simply a necklace) to be the equivalence class of a sequence of extended peaks under cyclic shift. Often it is more convenient for us to view a necklace as simply a collection of extended peaks with a given cyclic order; it will be clear from context when we do so. Let 𝖭𝖾𝖼𝗄n,k\mathsf{Neck}_{n,k} denote the set of all necklaces with kk extended peaks and a total of nn UU’s.

Let ψ\psi be the map taking a composition (μ1,μ2,…,μk)(\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\dots,\mu_{k}) of nn to the sequence S1S2⋯SkS_{1}S_{2}\cdots S_{k} of extended peaks where ℓ⁡(Si)=μi\ell(S_{i})=\mu_{i} for each ii. Note that ψ\psi is a bijection between compositions of nn with kk parts and sequences of kk extended peaks with a total of nn UU’s; moreover, ψ\psi induces a bijection—which we also denote ψ\psi by a slight abuse of notation—from 𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k\mathsf{CComp}_{n,k} to 𝖭𝖾𝖼𝗄n,k\mathsf{Neck}_{n,k}. To be precise, the necklace ψ⁡[μ]\psi[\mu] is the equivalence class of ψ⁡(μ¯)\psi(\bar{\mu}) for any μ¯∈[μ]\bar{\mu}\in[\mu], which clearly does not depend on the choice of representative.

We define a marking of a necklace of extended peaks [S1,…,Sk][S_{1},\ldots,S_{k}] to be the necklace [S1,…,Sk][S_{1},\ldots,S_{k}] with k−1k-1 UU’s marked. Given [μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n,k}, let 𝖬𝖭𝖾𝖼𝗄⁡[μ]\mathsf{MNeck}[\mu] be the set of all marked necklaces of extended peaks corresponding to the cyclic composition [μ][\mu]. If [μ][\mu] is primitive—that is, if 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]=k\mathsf{ord}[\mu]=k—then observe that the necklace ψ⁡[μ]\psi[\mu] has OPEN(nk−1CLOSE)\binom{n}{k-1} distinct markings. More generally, we have the following:

Lemma 3.2.

Given [μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n,k}, we have

|𝖬𝖭𝖾𝖼𝗄⁡[μ]|=𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]k​OPEN(nk−1CLOSE).\lvert\mathsf{MNeck}[\mu]\rvert=\frac{\mathsf{ord}[\mu]}{k}\binom{n}{k-1}.
Proof.

Let NN denote the necklace of extended peaks corresponding to [μ][\mu], and fix a sequence S1S2⋯Sk∈NS_{1}S_{2}\cdots S_{k}\in N of extended peaks. Then there are OPEN(nk−1CLOSE)\binom{n}{k-1} ways to choose the k−1k-1 UU’s to be marked in S1S2⋯SkS_{1}S_{2}\cdots S_{k}. Upon taking all kk cyclic shifts of S1S2⋯SkS_{1}S_{2}\cdots S_{k}, observe that each cyclic shift appears k/𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]k/\mathsf{ord}[\mu] times; accordingly, each of the markings counted by OPEN(nk−1CLOSE)\binom{n}{k-1} is k/𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]k/\mathsf{ord}[\mu] times the number of markings in 𝖬𝖭𝖾𝖼𝗄⁡[μ]\mathsf{MNeck}[\mu]. In other words, we have

k𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]​|𝖬𝖭𝖾𝖼𝗄⁡[μ]|=OPEN(nk−1CLOSE),\frac{k}{\mathsf{ord}[\mu]}\lvert\mathsf{MNeck}[\mu]\rvert=\binom{n}{k-1},

which is equivalent to our desired conclusion. ∎

A Dyck word π=π1⋯π2​n\pi=\pi_{1}\cdots\pi_{2n} with exactly kk U​DUD-factors can be expressed uniquely in the form π=Ua1Db1⋯UakDbk\pi=U^{a_{1}}D^{b_{1}}\cdots U^{a_{k}}D^{b_{k}}, where (a1,…,ak)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}) and (b1,…,bk)(b_{1},\ldots,b_{k}) are both compositions of nn. Let us call (a1,…,ak)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}) the rise composition of π\pi. Given a cyclic composition [μ][\mu], denote by 𝖣⁡[μ]\mathsf{D}[\mu] the set of all Dyck words with rise composition in the equivalence class [μ][\mu].

Lemma 3.3.

Given [μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n,k}, we have

(3.1) |𝖣⁡[μ]|=𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]k​OPEN(nk−1CLOSE).\lvert\mathsf{D}[\mu]\rvert=\frac{\mathsf{ord}[\mu]}{k}\binom{n}{k-1}.
Proof.

From Lemma  3.2, it suffices to find a bijection from 𝖬𝖭𝖾𝖼𝗄⁡[μ]\mathsf{MNeck}[\mu] to D⁡[μ]D[\mu].

Let [S]=[S1,S2,…,Sk]∈𝖬𝖭𝖾𝖼𝗄⁡[μ][S]=[S_{1},S_{2},\ldots,S_{k}]\in\mathsf{MNeck}[\mu]. We will choose a unique ordering of the marked extended peaks S1,S2,…,SkS_{1},S_{2},\ldots,S_{k}. To do this, we first record the k−1k-1 marked UU’s and kk extended peaks using a sequence of ○\bigcirc’s and □\square’s as follows. Starting with any extended peak SiS_{i}, record a ○\bigcirc for each marked UU on this extended peak, and then record a □\square for this extended peak. Repeat this procedure for the next extended peak in the cyclic order until all extended peaks and their markings have been recorded.

This gives a sequence consisting of k−1k-1 copies of ○\bigcirc and kk copies of □\square. It then follows from Corollary  2.3 that there is exactly one cyclic shift σ=σ1​σ2​…​σ2​k−1\sigma=\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\ldots\sigma_{2k-1} of this sequence where every proper prefix of σ\sigma has at least as many ○\bigcirc’s as the number of □\square’s. Note that σ1=○\sigma_{1}=\bigcirc and σ2​k−2​σ2​k−1=□​□\sigma_{2k-2}\sigma_{2k-1}=\square\square. Using σ\sigma, we obtain a unique ordering R1,R2,…,RkR_{1},R_{2},\ldots,R_{k} of the marked extended peaks of [S][S] by taking RiR_{i} to be the extended peak corresponding to the iith ○\bigcirc in σ\sigma, for every i∈[k]i\in[k]. As this choice of ordering does not depend on the representative of [S][S] chosen, the ordering R1,R2,…,RkR_{1},R_{2},\ldots,R_{k} of the marked extended peaks in [S][S] is well-defined.

For example, consider the representative (U¯​U​U¯​D,U​D,U​U​U​D,U¯​D)(\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\underline{U}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}U\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\underline{U}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}D,UD,UUUD,\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\underline{U}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}D) in the marked necklace [U¯​U​U¯​D,U​D,U​U​U​D,U¯​D]∈𝖬𝖭𝖾𝖼𝗄⁡[3,1,3,1][\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\underline{U}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}U\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\underline{U}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}D,UD,UUUD,\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\underline{U}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}D]\in\mathsf{MNeck}[3,1,3,1]. This is associated to the sequence ○○□□□○□\bigcirc\bigcirc\square\square\square\bigcirc\square with only the cyclic shift ○□○○□□□\bigcirc\square\bigcirc\bigcirc\square\square\square having at least as many ○\bigcirc’s as □\square’s in every proper prefix. Thus, R1=U¯​DR_{1}=\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\underline{U}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}D, R2=U¯​U​U¯​DR_{2}=\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\underline{U}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}U\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\underline{U}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}D, R3=U​DR_{3}=UD, and R4=U​U​U​DR_{4}=UUUD.

Given the sequence of extended peaks R1,R2,…,RkR_{1},R_{2},\ldots,R_{k}, we construct a Dyck word ww in the following manner.

  1. (1)

    Set w=Uℓ⁡(R1)w=U^{\ell(R_{1})} and mark the corresponding UU’s that are marked in R1R_{1}.

  2. (2)

    For the next RiR_{i} that has not been appended to ww, find the rightmost marked UU in ww, and let its position in ww be jj. Let cc be the number of UU’s from wjw_{j} to the end of ww inclusive that are not paired with a DD to their right. Append cc copies of DD to the end of ww followed by Uℓ⁡(Ri)U^{\ell(R_{i})}.

    Mark the corresponding UU’s in ww that were marked in RiR_{i} and unmark wjw_{j} in ww.

    Repeat steps (2)(2) and (3)(3) until we have appended all kk extended peaks.

For example, given R1=U¯​DR_{1}=\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\underline{U}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}D, R2=U¯​U​U¯​DR_{2}=\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\underline{U}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}U\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\underline{U}\color[rgb]{0,0,0}D, R3=U​DR_{3}=UD, and R4=U​U​U​DR_{4}=UUUD, the associated word ww is U​D​U​U​U​D​U​D​D​D​U​U​U​D​D​DUDUUUDUDDDUUUDDD.

Note that there will always be at least one marked UU to indicate how many DD’s must be added before the next extended peak because the number of marked UU’s (the ○\bigcirc’s) will always be at least the number of extended peaks (the □\square’s) that need attaching by the choice of ordering. Moreover, ww is a Dyck word as at every point in the construction of ww, the number of DD’s added are weakly less than the number of UU’s present in ww. The rise composition of ww is given by (ℓ⁡(R1),ℓ⁡(R2),…,ℓ⁡(Rk))(\ell(R_{1}),\ell(R_{2}),\ldots,\ell(R_{k})) which by construction is cyclically equivalent to μ\mu. Thus, ww is in 𝖣⁡[μ]\mathsf{D}[\mu].

Conversely, consider a Dyck word π=Ua1Db1⋯UakDbk\pi=U^{a_{1}}D^{b_{1}}\cdots U^{a_{k}}D^{b_{k}} whose rise composition (a1,a2,…,ak)(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{k}) is contained in the equivalence class [μ][\mu]. We decompose π\pi into a marked sequence of extended peaks (R1,R2,…,Rk)(R_{1},R_{2},\ldots,R_{k}) as follows.

    Set Rk=Uak​DR_{k}=U^{a_{k}}D with no markings and set ww to be the word π\pi with Uak​DbkU^{a_{k}}D^{b_{k}} deleted from its end.

By construction, we have ℓ⁡(Ri)=ai\ell(R_{i})=a_{i} for all 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k. Moreover, as π\pi is a Dyck word, the UU that is marked at the end of step (2)(2) must have been unmarked at the beginning of step (2)(2). Hence, R1,R2,…,RkR_{1},R_{2},\ldots,R_{k} have exactly k−1k-1 marked UU’s, and [R1,R2,…,Rk][R_{1},R_{2},\ldots,R_{k}] is an element of 𝖬𝖭𝖾𝖼𝗄⁡[μ]\mathsf{MNeck}[\mu].

It is straightforward to verify that the two procedures described above are inverse bijections between marked necklaces of extended peaks whose up-lengths are cyclically equivalent to μ\mu and Dyck words whose rise compositions are cyclically equivalent to μ\mu. Hence, the lemma follows. ∎

Let 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k,m\mathsf{Comp}_{n,k,m} denote the set of all compositions in 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k\mathsf{Comp}_{n,k} with exactly mm parts at least 22, and let 𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k,m\mathsf{CComp}_{n,k,m} be its cyclic counterpart. Using Lemma  3.3, we obtain a combinatorial proof for Theorem  1.2. The proof of the nontrivial case is given below.

Combinatorial proof of Theorem  1.2.

First, we take the Dyck paths counted by wn,k,mw_{n,k,m} and partition them by the cyclic equivalence classes of their rise compositions. Then we have

(3.2) wn,k,m=∑[μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k,m|D⁡[μ]|=∑[μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k,m𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]k​OPEN(nk−1CLOSE)w_{n,k,m}=\sum_{[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n,k,m}}\lvert D[\mu]\rvert=\sum_{[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n,k,m}}\frac{\mathsf{ord}[\mu]}{k}\binom{n}{k-1}

upon applying Lemma  3.3. Next, recall that every cyclic composition [μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k,m[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n,k,m} contains 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]\mathsf{ord}[\mu] distinct compositions in 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k,m\mathsf{Comp}_{n,k,m}, so we have

(3.3) wn,k,m=∑μ∈𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k,m1𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]​𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]k​OPEN(nk−1CLOSE)=1k​OPEN(nk−1CLOSE)​|𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k,m|.w_{n,k,m}=\sum_{\mu\in\mathsf{Comp}_{n,k,m}}\frac{1}{\mathsf{ord}[\mu]}\frac{\mathsf{ord}[\mu]}{k}\binom{n}{k-1}=\frac{1}{k}\binom{n}{k-1}\lvert\mathsf{Comp}_{n,k,m}\rvert.

Finally, we claim that

(3.4) |𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k,m|=OPEN(n−k−1m−1CLOSE)​OPEN(kmCLOSE);\lvert\mathsf{Comp}_{n,k,m}\rvert=\binom{n-k-1}{m-1}\binom{k}{m};

indeed, we can uniquely generate all compositions of nn into kk parts with exactly mm parts at least 2 using the following process:

  1. (1)

    Take the composition (1k)(1^{k}) consisting of kk copies of 1, and choose mm positions 1≤i1<i2<⋯<im≤k1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{m}\leq k within this composition; there are OPEN(kmCLOSE)\binom{k}{m} ways to do this.

  2. (2)

    Choose a composition μ=(μ1,μ2,…,μm)\mu=(\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\dots,\mu_{m}) of n−kn-k into mm parts; there are OPEN(n−k−1m−1CLOSE)\binom{n-k-1}{m-1} ways to do this.

Substituting (3.4) into (3.3) completes the proof. ∎

As a consequence of our combinatorial proof for Theorem  1.2, we also obtain a proof of Theorem  1.5 for the numbers wn,k1,k2,…,krw_{n,k_{1},k_{2},\ldots,k_{r}}.

3.2. Combinatorial proof of Theorem 1.3

Now, we focus our attention on finding a combinatorial proof of Theorem 1.3, which in turn will give a combinatorial proof of Theorem 1.1. See Figure  1 for an example of the symmetry in Theorem 1.1 that we wish to prove.

Our proof will mostly rely on two key results. The first gives a combinatorial interpretation for Narayana numbers in terms of cyclic compositions.

Lemma 3.4.

Let k≥1k\geq 1 and m≥0m\geq 0. Then the Narayana number Nk,mN_{k,m} is the number of cyclic compositions of 2​k+12k+1 into kk parts such that exactly mm parts are at least 2.

Proof.

We will give a bijective map that takes a cyclic composition of 2​k+12k+1 into kk parts, exactly mm of which are at least 22, to a Dyck path of semilength kk with mm U​DUD-factors, which are counted by the Narayana numbers Nk,mN_{k,m}.

Given a cyclic composition [μ1,μ2,…,μk][\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\ldots,\mu_{k}] of 2​k+12k+1 with exactly mm parts that are at least 22, consider the word Uμ1−1DUμ2−1D⋯Uμk−1DU^{\mu_{1}-1}DU^{\mu_{2}-1}D\cdots U^{\mu_{k}-1}D, which has k+1k+1 copies of UU and kk copies of DD. By the cycle lemma, there is exactly one cyclic shift of this word that is 11-dominating—that is, with more UU’s than DD’s in every prefix. Then the first two entries of this 11-dominating sequence are necessarily UU’s. Removing the first UU, we obtain a Dyck path of semilength kk with exactly mm U​DUD-factors.

It is easily verified that the inverse procedure is given by the following: from a semilength kk Dyck path with mm U​DUD-factors, we get a sequence (a1,a2,…,ak)(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{k}) where aia_{i} is the number of UU’s that immediately precede the iith DD. For example, from U​D​U​U​D​D​U​DUDUUDDUD we get the sequence (1,2,0,1)(1,2,0,1). Then we add 22 to a1a_{1} and 11 to each other aia_{i}, forming a composition μ\mu of 2​k+12k+1 into kk parts, exactly mm of which are at least 22. Taking the cyclic composition [μ][\mu] completes the inverse. ∎

We note that the map used in the proof of Lemma 3.4 is related to the standard bijection between Łukasiewicz paths and Dyck paths. A Łukasiewicz path of length nn is a path in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} with step set {(1,−1),(1,0),(1,1),(1,2),…}\{(1,-1),(1,0),(1,1),(1,2),\ldots\}, starting from (0,0)(0,0) and ending at (n,0)(n,0), that never traverses below the xx-axis; these paths were introduced in relation to the preorder degree sequence of a plane tree, which determines the tree unambiguously [16, Section 1.5.3].

As 2​k+12k+1 and kk are relatively prime, every cyclic composition of 𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​k+1,k\mathsf{CComp}_{2k+1,k} is primitive. Lemma  3.3 then gives us the following corollary.

Corollary 3.5.

Let k≥1k\geq 1. Given a cyclic composition [μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​k+1,k[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{2k+1,k}, there are exactly 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁(2​k+1k−1𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸)\binom{2k+1}{k-1} Dyck words whose rise composition belongs to [μ][\mu].

We are now ready to complete our combinatorial proof of Theorem 1.3.

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

Recall that w2​k+1,k,mw_{2k+1,k,m} counts Dyck words of semilength 2​k+12k+1, kk U​DUD-factors, and mm U​U​DUUD-factors; these are precisely the Dyck words of semilength 2​k+12k+1 whose rise composition has kk parts with exactly mm parts having size at least 2. These rise compositions can be grouped into cyclic compositions of 2​k+12k+1 having kk total parts and mm parts at least 2, which are counted by Nk,mN_{k,m} as established in Lemma 3.4. Furthermore, by Lemma 3.5, there are exactly OPEN(2​k+1k−1CLOSE)\binom{2k+1}{k-1} Dyck words corresponding to each such cyclic composition. It follows that w2​k+1,k,m=OPEN(2​k+1k−1CLOSE)​Nk,mw_{2k+1,k,m}=\binom{2k+1}{k-1}N_{k,m} as desired. ∎

From the proofs of Lemmas  3.3 and  3.4, we implicitly obtain a bijection that demonstrates the symmetry w2​k+1,k,m=w2​k+1,k,k+1−mw_{2k+1,k,m}=w_{2k+1,k,k+1-m}. For the sake of completeness, we explicitly write out the bijection that we obtain and give an example in Figure  2.

Definition 3.6.

Let π\pi be a Dyck word with semilength 2​k+12k+1, kk U​DUD-factors, and mm U​U​DUUD-factors. Construct a Dyck word π′\pi^{\prime} with semilength 2​k+12k+1, kk U​DUD-factors, and k+1−mk+1-m U​U​DUUD-factors via the following algorithm:

  1. (1)

    Set MM to be the marked necklace of extended peaks associated to π\pi via Lemma  3.3.

  2. (2)

    Decompose MM into a pair consisting of its underlying unmarked necklace of extended peaks NN and a (k−1)(k-1)-subset SS of [2​k+1]={1,2,…,2​k+1}[2k+1]=\{1,2,\dots,2k+1\} containing the positions of the UU’s marked in MM.

  3. (3)

    Set PP to be the Dyck path of semilength kk with mm U​DUD-factors that is associated to NN via the bijective map in Lemma  3.4.

  4. (4)

    Set P′P^{\prime} to be a Dyck path of semilength kk with k+1−mk+1-m U​DUD-factors obtained via any bijection demonstrating the Narayana symmetry (see [18, 19, 20] for example). Perhaps the simplest and most intuitive is the one in terms of non-crossing set partitions in [19], where the author proved the stronger fact that the lattice of non-crossing partitions is self-dual.

  5. (5)

    Set N′N^{\prime} to be the necklace of extended peaks associated to P′P^{\prime} via Lemma 3.4.

  6. (6)

    Set M′M^{\prime} to be the marked necklace of extended peaks obtained from the necklace N′N^{\prime} and subset SS.

  7. (7)

    Set π′\pi^{\prime} to be the Dyck word with semilength 2​k+12k+1, kk U​DUD-factors, and k+1−mk+1-m U​U​DUUD-factors associated with M′M^{\prime} via Lemma 3.3.

Remark 3.7.

In Steps (2) and (6), there is some choice of how to label the positions of the UU’s in a necklace N∈𝖭𝖾𝖼𝗄2​k+1,kN\in\mathsf{Neck}_{2k+1,k} such that one can pass from a marked necklace to a pair consisting of its underlying unmarked necklace and a (k−1)(k-1)-subset of [2​k+1][2k+1] and vice versa. We detail a choice of labeling that we deem to be canonical. By Lemma  2.2, there is a unique ordering (S1,S2,…,Sk)(S_{1},S_{2},\ldots,S_{k}) of the extended peaks in NN such that Uμ1−1DUμ2−1D⋯Uμk−1DU^{\mu_{1}-1}DU^{\mu_{2}-1}D\cdots U^{\mu_{k}-1}D is 11-dominating where μi=ℓ⁡(Ni)\mu_{i}=\ell(N_{i}). Starting from the leftmost UU, label the UU’s in N1N_{1} with the numbers 1,2,…,μ11,2,\ldots,\mu_{1}, label the UU’s in N2N_{2} with the numbers μ1+1,…,μ1+μ2\mu_{1}+1,\ldots,\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}, and so on.

3.3. Combinatorial proof of a related symmetry

In addition to the symmetry in Theorem 1.1, it can also be observed that w2​k−1,k,m=w2​k−1,k,k−mw_{2k-1,k,m}=w_{2k-1,k,k-m} for all 1≤m≤k1\leq m\leq k, which is a consequence of the following variation of Theorem 1.3.

Theorem 3.8.

For all k≥1k\geq 1 and m≥0m\geq 0, we have

(3.5) w2​k−1,k,m=OPEN(2​k−1k−1CLOSE)​Nk−1,m.w_{2k-1,k,m}=\binom{2k-1}{k-1}N_{k-1,m}.

Theorem 3.8 can be proven in a way that is completely analogous to our combinatorial proof of Theorem 1.3, but relying on Lemma 3.9 and Corollary 3.10 below.

Lemma 3.9.

Let k≥1k\geq 1 and m≥0m\geq 0. Then the Narayana number Nk−1,mN_{k-1,m} is the number of cyclic compositions of 2​k−12k-1 into kk parts such that exactly mm parts are at least 2.

Proof.

We follow the proof of Lemma 3.4 closely. Given a cyclic composition [μ1,μ2,…,μk][\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\ldots,\mu_{k}] of 2​k−12k-1 with exactly mm parts that are at least 22, we build a sequence consisting of k−1k-1 copies of UU and kk copies of DD in the same way as in the proof of Lemma 3.4. By Corollary 2.3, there is exactly one cyclic shift of this sequence such that any proper prefix of the sequence contains at least as many UU’s as the number of DD’s. Then the last entry of this cyclic shift is a DD; removing this last DD, we obtain a Dyck path of semilength k−1k-1 and exactly mm U​DUD-factors.

Conversely, consider a Dyck path of semilength k−1k-1 with exactly mm U​DUD-factors. We append a DD to the corresponding Dyck word, and form the sequence a1,a2,…,aka_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{k}, where aia_{i} is the number of UUs that immediately precede the iith DD. We then add 11 to every number in this sequence and take the equivalence class of its cyclic shifts, yielding a cyclic composition of 2​k−12k-1 into kk parts, exactly mm of which are at least 22. ∎

As 2​k−12k-1 and kk are relatively prime, Lemma  3.3 gives us the analogous corollary to Corollary  3.5.

Corollary 3.10.

Let k≥1k\geq 1. Given a cyclic composition [μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​k−1,k[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{2k-1,k}, there are exactly 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁(2​k−1k−1𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸)\binom{2k-1}{k-1} Dyck words whose rise composition belongs to [μ][\mu].

Using Lemma  3.3 and the proofs of Lemmas  3.4 and 3.9, we obtain a proof of Theorem  1.4 regarding a symmetry on the numbers wn,k1,k2,…,krw_{n,k_{1},k_{2},\ldots,k_{r}}.

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

Let μ∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉r​k+1,k,k,…,k,m\mu\in\mathsf{CComp}_{rk+1,k,k,\ldots,k,m}. From Lemma  3.3, we have D⁡[μ]=OPEN(r​k+1k−1CLOSE)D[\mu]=\binom{rk+1}{k-1} as [μ][\mu] must be primitive. Note that |𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉r​k+1,k,k,…,k,m|=Nk,m\lvert\mathsf{CComp}_{rk+1,k,k,\ldots,k,m}\rvert=N_{k,m} which can be shown via an argument analogous to that in the proof of Lemma  3.4. Thus, we have wr​k+1,k,k,…,k,m=OPEN(nk−1CLOSE)​Nk,mw_{rk+1,k,k,\ldots,k,m}=\binom{n}{k-1}N_{k,m}, which gives the desired symmetry in light of the Narayana symmetry. The symmetry for the numbers wr​k−1,k,k,…,k,mw_{rk-1,k,k,\ldots,k,m} can be proven similarly. ∎

4. Further generalizations and applications

We now detail several interesting generalizations and applications that can be obtained from our results in Section  3.

4.1. Catalan identity

First, we obtain a formula for the Catalan numbers CnC_{n} in terms of primitive cyclic compositions via Lemma  3.3.

Corollary 4.1.

For all n≥1n\geq 1, we have

Cn=1n+1​OPEN(2​nnCLOSE)=∑d|n∑[μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n/dprimitive1d​OPEN(n𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]⋅d−1CLOSE),C_{n}=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}=\sum_{d|n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{[\mu]}\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n/d}\\ \mathrm{primitive}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{d}\binom{n}{\mathsf{ord}[\mu]\cdot d-1},

where 𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n\mathsf{CComp}_{n} is the set of all cyclic compositions of nn.

Proof.

Grouping Dyck paths by their cyclic rise composition, we have

Cn=∑[μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉nD⁡[μ].C_{n}=\sum_{[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n}}D[\mu].

Recall that every cyclic composition of nn can be uniquely expressed as the concatenation of dd copies of a primitive cyclic composition of n/dn/d for some divisor dd of nn. Similarly, for every divisor dd of nn, each primitive cyclic composition of n/dn/d can be made into a cyclic composition of nn by concatenating dd copies. This gives us

Cn=∑[μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉nD⁡[μ]=∑d|n∑[μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n/dprimitiveD⁡([μ]d)C_{n}=\sum_{[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n}}D[\mu]=\sum_{d|n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n/d}\\ \text{primitive}\end{subarray}}D([\mu]^{d})

where [μ]d[\mu]^{d} is the concatenation of dd copies of [μ][\mu]. From Lemma  3.3, this gives us precisely

Cn=∑d|n∑[μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n/dprimitiveD⁡([μ]d)=∑d|n∑[μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n/dprimitive1d​OPEN(n𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]⋅d−1CLOSE).∎C_{n}=\sum_{d|n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n/d}\\ \text{primitive}\end{subarray}}D([\mu]^{d})=\sum_{d|n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{[\mu]}\in\mathsf{CComp}_{n/d}\\ \text{primitive}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{d}\binom{n}{\mathsf{ord}[\mu]\cdot d-1}.\qed

4.2. Generalized Narayana identities

Next, we generalize Theorems  1.3 and 3.8 by expressing the numbers wn,k,mw_{n,k,m}, for any n≠2​kn\neq 2k, in terms of a family of generalized Narayana numbers due to Callan  [8].

Given 0≤r≤n0\leq r\leq n and 0≤k≤n−r0\leq k\leq n-r, define the rr-generalized Narayana number Nn,k(r)N_{n,k}^{(r)} by

Nn,k(r)=r+1n+1​OPEN(n+1kCLOSE)​OPEN(n−r−1k−1CLOSE).N_{n,k}^{(r)}=\frac{r+1}{n+1}\binom{n+1}{k}\binom{n-r-1}{k-1}.

Observe that the usual Narayana numbers Nn,kN_{n,k} can be obtained by setting r=0r=0 in Nn,k(r)N_{n,k}^{(r)}. For k<0k<0, we use the convention that OPEN(nkCLOSE)=0\binom{n}{k}=0 except for the special case when n=k=−1n=k=-1, where we define OPEN(−1−1CLOSE)\binom{-1}{-1} to be 11.

The following is a generalization of Theorems 1.3 and 3.8.

Theorem 4.2.

For all j,k≥1j,k\geq 1 and m≥0m\geq 0, we have

w2​k+j,k,m=1j​OPEN(2​k+jk−1CLOSE)​Nk+j−1,m(j−1)w_{2k+j,k,m}=\frac{1}{j}\binom{2k+j}{k-1}N^{(j-1)}_{k+j-1,m}

and for all 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k and m≥0m\geq 0, we have

w2​k−j,k,m=1j​OPEN(2​k−jk−1CLOSE)​Nk−1,m(j−1).w_{2k-j,k,m}=\frac{1}{j}\binom{2k-j}{k-1}N^{(j-1)}_{k-1,m}.

Before proving Theorem  4.2, we first introduce a generalization of Dyck paths and prove a useful lemma. Consider paths in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} from (0,0)(0,0) to (2​n−r,r)(2n-r,r), consisting of nn up steps (1,1)(1,1) and n−rn-r down steps (1,−1)(1,-1), that never pass below the horizontal axis. Denote by Dn,k(r)D^{(r)}_{n,k} the set of words on the alphabet {U,D}\{U,D\} corresponding to such paths with exactly kk U​DUD-factors. In [8], Callan describes a proof by Schulte showing that Nn,k(r)N_{n,k}^{(r)} is the cardinality of Dn,k(r)D^{(r)}_{n,k}.

For ω,ν∈Dn,k(r)\omega,\nu\in D^{(r)}_{n,k}, let us write ω∼ν\omega\sim\nu if the words U​ωU\omega and U​νU\nu are cyclic shifts of each other. The relation ∼\sim is an equivalence relation on Dn,k(r)D^{(r)}_{n,k}, and we denote the set of its equivalence classes by D~n,k(r)\tilde{D}^{(r)}_{n,k}. For [ω]∈D~n,k(r)[\omega]\in\tilde{D}^{(r)}_{n,k}, let 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[ω]\mathsf{ord}[\omega] be the number of distinct elements of Dn,k(r)D^{(r)}_{n,k} contained within the equivalence class [ω][\omega].

Definition 4.3.

For j,k≥1j,k\geq 1, let ϕj,k\phi_{j,k} be the map from 𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​k+j,k,m\mathsf{CComp}_{2k+j,k,m} to D~k+j−1,m(j−1)\tilde{D}^{(j-1)}_{k+j-1,m} where ϕj,k​[μ]\phi_{j,k}[\mu] is obtained via the following algorithm:

  1. (1)

    For [μ]=[μ1,…,μk]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​k+j,k,m[\mu]=[\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{k}]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{2k+j,k,m}, set ω=Uμ1−1DUμ2−1D⋯Uμk−1D\omega=U^{\mu_{1}-1}DU^{\mu_{2}-1}D\cdots U^{\mu_{k}-1}D.

  2. (2)

    Let ν=ν1ν2⋯ν2​k+j\nu=\nu_{1}\nu_{2}\cdots\nu_{2k+j} be any cyclic shift of ω\omega that is 11-dominating.

  3. (3)

    Set ϕj,k​[μ]\phi_{j,k}[\mu] to be the equivalence class of the subword ν2⋯ν2​k+j\nu_{2}\cdots\nu_{2k+j}.

It is not immediately clear from the above definition whether the map ϕj,k\phi_{j,k} is well-defined, but this will be established in the proof of the following lemma.

Lemma 4.4.

For all j,k≥1j,k\geq 1, the map ϕj,k\phi_{j,k} is a bijection. Moreover, for all [μ]∈𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​k+j,k,m[\mu]\in\mathsf{CComp}_{2k+j,k,m}, we have

𝗈𝗋𝖽​(ϕj,k​[μ])𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]=jk.\frac{\mathsf{ord}(\phi_{j,k}[\mu])}{\mathsf{ord}[\mu]}=\frac{j}{k}.
Proof.

We first prove that ϕj,k\phi_{j,k} is well-defined. Since ω\omega contains k+jk+j copies of UU and kk copies of DD, the cycle lemma guarantees that at least one cyclic shift of ω\omega is 11-dominating. By construction of ω\omega, the word ν\nu must contain exactly mm U​DUD-factors. The fact that ν\nu is 11-dominating and contains mm U​DUD-factors implies that its subword ν2⋯ν2​k+j\nu_{2}\cdots\nu_{2k+j} is an element of Dk+j−1,m(j−1)D^{(j-1)}_{k+j-1,m}. From the definition of ∼\sim on Dk+j−1,m(j−1)D^{(j-1)}_{k+j-1,m}, any 11-dominating cyclic shift of ω\omega will be sent to the same equivalence class in D~k+j−1,m(j−1)\tilde{D}^{(j-1)}_{k+j-1,m}. This same argument also implies that ϕj,k​[μ]\phi_{j,k}[\mu] does not depend on the representative of [μ][\mu] that is chosen.

Injectivity and surjectivity are straightforward to check from the definition of ϕj,k\phi_{j,k}. By the cycle lemma, there are exactly jj cyclic shifts of ω\omega that are 11-dominating; among these jj words, there are j⋅𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]/kj\cdot\mathsf{ord}[\mu]/k distinct cyclic shifts as each of them appears k/𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]k/\mathsf{ord}[\mu] times. These 11-dominating sequences are in bijection with paths in the equivalence class of ϕj,k​[μ]\phi_{j,k}[\mu] by removing the first UU from the sequence. Thus, 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡(ϕj,k​[μ])=j⋅𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡[μ]/k\mathsf{ord}(\phi_{j,k}[\mu])=j\cdot\mathsf{ord}[\mu]/k. ∎

We are now ready to prove Theorem  4.2.

Proof of Theorem  4.2.

From Lemma  4.4, we have

|𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​k+j,k,m|=kj​|Dk+j−1,m(j−1)|=kj​Nk+j−1,m(j−1).\lvert\mathsf{Comp}_{2k+j,k,m}\rvert=\frac{k}{j}\lvert D^{(j-1)}_{k+j-1,m}\rvert=\frac{k}{j}N^{(j-1)}_{k+j-1,m}.

Substituting this into  (3.3) gives the desired result

w2​k+j,k,m=1j​OPEN(2​k+jk−1CLOSE)​Nk+j−1,m(j−1).w_{2k+j,k,m}=\frac{1}{j}\binom{2k+j}{k-1}N^{(j-1)}_{k+j-1,m}.

The proof for w2​k−j,k,mw_{2k-j,k,m} follows similarly by defining an analogous map φj,k\varphi_{j,k} from 𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​k−j,k,m\mathsf{CComp}_{2k-j,k,m} to D~k−1,m(j−1)\tilde{D}^{(j-1)}_{k-1,m} and reproving Lemma  4.4 for φj,k\varphi_{j,k}. ∎

Lemma  4.4 naturally leads to the following generalization of Lemmas  3.4 and  3.9, which expresses the number of cyclic compositions in 𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​k±j,k,m\mathsf{CComp}_{2k\pm j,k,m} in terms of rr-generalized Narayana numbers. Below, φ\varphi denotes Euler’s totient function.

Proposition 4.5.

Let k≥1k\geq 1 and m,j≥0m,j\geq 0, and let d=𝗀𝖼𝖽⁡(k,m,j)d=\mathsf{gcd}(k,m,j).22 2 If m=0m=0 or j=0j=0, then 𝗀𝖼𝖽⁡(k,m,j)\mathsf{gcd}(k,m,j) is defined to be the greatest common divisor of the nonzero numbers among kk, mm, and jj.

  1. (a)

    If j≥1j\geq 1, we have |𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​k+j,k,m|=1j​∑s|dφ⁡(s)​N(k+j)/s−1,m/s(j/s−1)\displaystyle{\lvert\mathsf{CComp}_{2k+j,k,m}\rvert=\frac{1}{j}\sum_{s\mid d}\varphi(s)N^{(j/s-1)}_{(k+j)/s-1,\,m/s}}.

  2. (b)

    If j=0j=0, we have |𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​k,k,m|=1k​∑s|dφ⁡(s)​OPEN(ks−1ms−1CLOSE)​OPEN(ksmsCLOSE)\displaystyle{\lvert\mathsf{CComp}_{2k,k,m}\rvert=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{s\mid d}\varphi(s)\binom{\frac{k}{s}-1}{\frac{m}{s}-1}\binom{\frac{k}{s}}{\frac{m}{s}}}.

  3. (c)

    If 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k, we have |𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​k−j,k,m|=1j​∑s|dφ⁡(s)​Nk/s−1,m/s(j/s−1)\displaystyle{\lvert\mathsf{CComp}_{2k-j,k,m}\rvert=\frac{1}{j}\sum_{s\mid d}\varphi(s)N^{(j/s-1)}_{k/s-1,\,m/s}}.

Let us call an (ordinary) composition μ\mu primitive if [μ][\mu] is primitive, and let 𝖯𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k,m\mathsf{PComp}_{n,k,m} denote the set of primitive compositions of nn with kk parts with exactly mm parts at least two. f⁡(ℓ)=|𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉(2​k+j)​ℓ/d,k​ℓ/d,m​ℓ/d|andg⁡(ℓ)=|𝖯𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉(2​k+j)​ℓ/d,k​ℓ/d,m​ℓ/d|.f(\ell)=\lvert\mathsf{Comp}_{(2k+j)\ell/d,\,k\ell/d,\,m\ell/d}\rvert\quad\text{and}\quad g(\ell)=\lvert\mathsf{PComp}_{(2k+j)\ell/d,\,k\ell/d,\,m\ell/d}\rvert.

after all, every cyclic composition in 𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​k+j,k,m\mathsf{CComp}_{2k+j,k,m} is a concatenation of ℓ\ell copies of a primitive cyclic composition with k/ℓk/\ell parts for some ℓ\ell dividing dd, and this primitive cyclic composition is the cyclic equivalence class of k/ℓk/\ell elements of 𝖯𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉(2​k+j)/ℓ,k/ℓ,m/ℓ\mathsf{PComp}_{(2k+j)/\ell,\,k/\ell,\,m/\ell}. We then have

|𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​k+j,k,m|\displaystyle\lvert\mathsf{CComp}_{2k+j,k,m}\rvert =∑ℓ|dℓk​|𝖯𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉(2​k+j)/ℓ,k/ℓ,m/ℓ|\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell\mid d}\frac{\ell}{k}\lvert\mathsf{PComp}_{(2k+j)/\ell,\,k/\ell,\,m/\ell}\rvert

=1k​∑s|dφ⁡(s)​f​(ds),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{s\mid d}\varphi(s)f\Big(\frac{d}{s}\Big),

where the last step uses the well-known identity φ⁡(s)=∑q|s𝖬​𝗈¨​𝖻​(q)​s/q\varphi(s)=\sum_{q\mid s}\mathsf{M\ddot{o}b}(q)s/q. If j≥1j\geq 1, then we have

f⁡(ds)=|𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉2​(k/s)+j/s,k/s,m/s|=kj​N(k+j)/s−1,m/s(j/s−1)f\Big(\frac{d}{s}\Big)=\lvert\mathsf{Comp}_{2(k/s)+j/s,\,k/s,\,m/s}\rvert=\frac{k}{j}N^{(j/s-1)}_{(k+j)/s-1,\,m/s}

Remark 4.6.

Proposition  4.5 has an interesting interpretation related to permutation enumeration, as |𝖢𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉n,k,m|\lvert\mathsf{CComp}_{n,k,m}\rvert is the number of distinct cyclic descent sets among cyclic permutations of length nn with kk cyclic descents and mm cyclic peaks (for all 1≤k<n1\leq k<n); see [13, 14, 22, 23] for definitions. In particular, when j≠0j\neq 0 and 𝗀𝖼𝖽⁡(k,j,m)=1\mathsf{gcd}(k,j,m)=1, the number of cyclic descent classes among such cyclic permutations of length 2​k+j2k+j is equal to a generalized Narayana number divided by jj. The case j=±1j=\pm 1 (Lemmas  3.4 and  3.9) yields a new interpretation of the (ordinary) Narayana numbers Nk,mN_{k,m} in terms of cyclic descent classes.

5. Polynomials

5.1. Real-rootedness

A natural question is whether or not the sequence {wn,k,m}0≤m≤k\{w_{n,k,m}\}_{0\leq m\leq k}, for a fixed nn and kk, is unimodal. In other words, for fixed nn and kk, does there always exist 0≤j≤k0\leq j\leq k such that

wn,k,0≤wn,k,1≤⋯≤wn,k,j≥wn,k,j+1≥⋯≥wn,k,k​?w_{n,k,0}\leq w_{n,k,1}\leq\cdots\leq w_{n,k,j}\geq w_{n,k,j+1}\geq\cdots\geq w_{n,k,k}?

One way to prove unimodality results in combinatorics is through real-rootedness. A polynomial with coefficients in ℝ\mathbb{R} is said to be real-rooted if all of its roots are in ℝ\mathbb{R}. (We use the convention that constant polynomials are also real-rooted.) It is well known that if a polynomial with non-negative coefficients is real-rooted, then the sequence of its coefficients is unimodal (see  [6], for example).

Let Wn,k​(t)W_{n,k}(t) be the polynomial defined by

Wn,k​(t)=∑m=0kwn,k,m​tm.\displaystyle W_{n,k}(t)=\sum_{m=0}^{k}w_{n,k,m}t^{m}.

In what follows, we prove that the polynomials Wn,k​(t)W_{n,k}(t) are real-rooted, thus implying the unimodality of the sequences {wn,k,m}0≤m≤k\{w_{n,k,m}\}_{0\leq m\leq k}.

We begin with a simple result involving the roots of Wn,k​(t)W_{n,k}(t).

Proposition 5.1.

For all 1≤k≤n−11\leq k\leq n-1, the polynomials Wn,k​(t)W_{n,k}(t) and Wn,n−k​(t)W_{n,n-k}(t) have the same roots.

Proof.

This follows from the fact that wn,k,m=k⁡(k+1)(n−k)​(n−k+1)​wn,n−k,mw_{n,k,m}=\frac{k(k+1)}{(n-k)(n-k+1)}w_{n,n-k,m}, which is readily verified from Theorem  1.2. ∎

To prove the real-rootedness of the Wn,k​(t)W_{n,k}(t), we make use of Malo’s result regarding the roots of the Hadamard product of two real-rooted polynomials.

Theorem 5.2 ([24]).

Let f⁡(t)=∑i=0mai​tif(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{m}a_{i}t^{i} and g⁡(t)=∑i=0nbi​tig(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}b_{i}t^{i} be real-rooted polynomials in ℝ⁡[t]\mathbb{R}[t] such that all the roots of gg have the same sign. Then their Hadamard product

f∗g=∑i=0ℓai​bi​ti,f\ast g=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell}a_{i}b_{i}t^{i},

where ℓ=min⁡{m,n}\ell=\min\{m,n\}, is real-rooted.

Theorem 5.3.

For all n,k≥0n,k\geq 0, the polynomials Wn,k​(t)W_{n,k}(t) are real-rooted.

Proof.

From Theorem  1.2, we have

(5.1) Wn,k​(t)={0, if ​n<k,1, if ​n=k,1k​OPEN(nk−1CLOSE)​∑m=1min​{k,n−k}OPEN(n−k−1m−1CLOSE)​OPEN(kmCLOSE)​tm, if ​n>k.W_{n,k}(t)=\begin{cases}0,&\text{ if }n<k,\\ 1,&\text{ if }n=k,\\ \frac{1}{k}\binom{n}{k-1}\sum_{m=1}^{\text{min}\{k,n-k\}}\binom{n-k-1}{m-1}\binom{k}{m}t^{m},&\text{ if }n>k.\end{cases}

Thus it suffices to check that the polynomial ∑m=1min​{k,n−k}OPEN(n−k−1m−1CLOSE)​OPEN(kmCLOSE)​tm\sum_{m=1}^{\text{min}\{k,n-k\}}\binom{n-k-1}{m-1}\binom{k}{m}t^{m} is real-rooted, which follows from applying Theorem  5.2 to f⁡(t)=t​(t−1)n−k−1f(t)=t(t-1)^{n-k-1} and g⁡(t)=(t−1)kg(t)=(t-1)^{k}. ∎

More generally, we conjecture the polynomials Wn,k​(t)W_{n,k}(t) satisfy stronger conditions which we presently define. For two real-rooted polynomials ff and gg, let {ui}\{u_{i}\} be the roots of ff and {vi}\{v_{i}\} the roots of gg, both in non-increasing order. We say that gg interlaces ff, denoted by g→fg\rightarrow f, if either deg⁡(f)=deg⁡(g)+1=d\deg(f)=\deg(g)+1=d and

ud≤vd−1≤ud−1≤⋯≤v1≤u1,u_{d}\leq v_{d-1}\leq u_{d-1}\leq\cdots\leq v_{1}\leq u_{1},

or if deg⁡(f)=deg⁡(g)=d\deg(f)=\deg(g)=d and

vd≤ud≤vd−1≤ud−1≤⋯≤v1≤u1.v_{d}\leq u_{d}\leq v_{d-1}\leq u_{d-1}\leq\cdots\leq v_{1}\leq u_{1}.

(By convention, we assume that a constant polynomial interlaces with every real-rooted polynomial.) We say that a sequence of real-rooted polynomials f1,f2,…f_{1},f_{2},\ldots is a Sturm sequence if f1→f2→⋯.f_{1}\rightarrow f_{2}\rightarrow\cdots. Moreover, a finite sequence of real-rooted polynomials f1,f2,…,fnf_{1},f_{2},\ldots,f_{n} is said to be Sturm-unimodal if there exists 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n such that

f1→f2→⋯→fj←fj+1←⋯←fn.f_{1}\rightarrow f_{2}\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow\ f_{j}\leftarrow f_{j+1}\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow f_{n}.
Conjecture 5.4.

For any fixed k≥1k\geq 1, the polynomials {Wn,k​(t)}n≥k\{W_{n,k}(t)\}_{n\geq k} form a Sturm sequence.

Conjecture 5.5.

For any fixed n≥1n\geq 1, the sequence {Wn,k​(t)}1≤k≤n\{W_{n,k}(t)\}_{1\leq k\leq n} is Sturm-unimodal.

We note that Conjectures 5.4 and 5.5 were originally posed in previous versions of this paper; since their appearance, these conjectures have been resolved in [28].

Our result expressing the numbers wn,k,mw_{n,k,m} in terms of generalized Narayana numbers has a natural polynomial analogue. Let Nark(r)⁡(t)\operatorname{Nar}^{(r)}_{k}(t) denote the kkth rr-generalized Narayana polynomial defined by

Nark(r)⁡(t)=∑m=0k−rNk,m(r)​tm=r+1k+1​∑m=0k−rOPEN(k+1mCLOSE)​OPEN(k−r−1m−1CLOSE)​tm.\operatorname{Nar}^{(r)}_{k}(t)=\sum_{m=0}^{k-r}N^{(r)}_{k,m}t^{m}=\frac{r+1}{k+1}\sum_{m=0}^{k-r}\binom{k+1}{m}\binom{k-r-1}{m-1}t^{m}.

Setting r=0r=0 recovers the usual Narayana polynomials Nark⁡(t)=∑m=0kNk,m​tm\operatorname{Nar}_{k}(t)=\sum_{m=0}^{k}N_{k,m}t^{m}. From Theorem  4.2 and straightforward computations, we have the following expressions for Wn,k​(t)W_{n,k}(t).

Proposition 5.6.

Let k≥1k\geq 1.

  1. (a)

    For all j≥1j\geq 1, we have W2​k+j,k​(t)=1j​OPEN(2​k+jk−1CLOSE)​Nark+j−1(j−1)⁡(t)\displaystyle{W_{2k+j,k}(t)=\frac{1}{j}\binom{2k+j}{k-1}\operatorname{Nar}^{(j-1)}_{k+j-1}(t)}.

  2. (b)

    We have W2​k,k​(t)=Ck​∑m=1kOPEN(k−1m−1CLOSE)​OPEN(kmCLOSE)​tm\displaystyle{W_{2k,k}(t)=C_{k}\sum_{m=1}^{k}\binom{k-1}{m-1}\binom{k}{m}t^{m}} where CkC_{k} denotes the kkth Catalan number.

  3. (c)

    For all 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k, we have W2​k−j,k​(t)=1j​OPEN(2​k−jk−1CLOSE)​Nark−1(j−1)⁡(t)\displaystyle{W_{2k-j,k}(t)=\frac{1}{j}\binom{2k-j}{k-1}\operatorname{Nar}^{(j-1)}_{k-1}(t)}.

The real-rootedness of the rr-generalized Narayana polynomials was recently shown in [9] using a different approach; Proposition 5.6 shows that the real-rootedness of the Wn,k​(t)W_{n,k}(t) implies the real-rootedness of the Nark(r)⁡(t)\operatorname{Nar}^{(r)}_{k}(t), thus giving an alternative proof of this result.

5.2. Symmetry, γ\gamma-positivity, and a symmetric decomposition

It is fitting that we end this paper by returning full circle to the topic of symmetry. A polynomial a0+a1​t+⋯+ad​tda_{0}+a_{1}t+\cdots+a_{d}t^{d} of degree dd is said to be symmetric if ai=ad−ia_{i}=a_{d-i} for all 0≤i≤d0\leq i\leq d. First, we note that our symmetries for the numbers w2​k+1,k,mw_{2k+1,k,m} and w2​k−1,k,mw_{2k-1,k,m} immediately imply the following:

Proposition 5.7.

The polynomials W2​k+1,k​(t)W_{2k+1,k}(t) and W2​k−1,k​(t)W_{2k-1,k}(t) are symmetric.

A symmetric polynomial of degree dd can be written uniquely as a linear combination of the polynomials {tj​(1+t)d−2​j}0≤j≤⌊d/2⌋\{t^{j}(1+t)^{d-2j}\}_{0\leq j\leq\lfloor d/2\rfloor}, referred to as the gamma basis. A symmetric polynomial is called γ\gamma-positive if its coefficients in the gamma basis are nonnegative. Gamma-positivity has shown up in many combinatorial and geometric contexts; see [1] for a thorough survey. It is well known that the coefficients of a γ\gamma-positive polynomial form a unimodal sequence, and that γ\gamma-positivity is connected to real-rootedness in the following manner:

Theorem 5.8 ([4]).

If ff is a real-rooted, symmetric polynomial with nonnegative coefficients, then ff is γ\gamma-positive.

The γ\gamma-positivity of the polynomials W2​k+1,k​(t)W_{2k+1,k}(t) and W2​k−1,k​(t)W_{2k-1,k}(t) then follows directly from Theorem  5.3, Proposition 5.7, and Theorem 5.8. Furthermore, we can get explicit formulas for their gamma coefficients by exploiting their connection to the Narayana polynomials.

Proposition 5.9.

The polynomials W2​k+1,k​(t)W_{2k+1,k}(t) and W2​k−1,k​(t)W_{2k-1,k}(t) are γ\gamma-positive for all k≥1k\geq 1. More precisely, we have the following gamma expansions:

  1. (a)

    W2​k+1,k​(t)=∑j=1⌊k+12⌋OPEN(2​k+1k−1CLOSE)​(k−1)!(k−2​j+1)!​(j−1)!​j!​tj​(1+t)k+1−2​j\displaystyle{W_{2k+1,k}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{k+1}{2}\rfloor}\binom{2k+1}{k-1}\frac{(k-1)!}{(k-2j+1)!\,(j-1)!\,j!}\,t^{j}(1+t)^{k+1-2j}} for all k≥1k\geq 1;

  2. (b)

    W2​k−1,k​(t)=∑j=1⌊k+12⌋OPEN(2​k−1k−1CLOSE)​(k−2)!(k−2​j)!​(j−1)!​j!​tj​(1+t)k+1−2​j\displaystyle{W_{2k-1,k}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{k+1}{2}\rfloor}\binom{2k-1}{k-1}\frac{(k-2)!}{(k-2j)!\,(j-1)!\,j!}\,t^{j}(1+t)^{k+1-2j}} for all k≥2k\geq 2.

Proof.

The Narayana polynomials are known to be γ\gamma-positive with gamma expansion

Nark⁡(t)=∑j=1⌊k+12⌋(k−1)!(k−2​j+1)!​(j−1)!​j!​tj​(1+t)k+1−2​j\operatorname{Nar}_{k}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor\frac{k+1}{2}\rfloor}\frac{(k-1)!}{(k-2j+1)!\,(j-1)!\,j!}\,t^{j}(1+t)^{k+1-2j}

for all k≥1k\geq 1 [1, Theorem 2.32], and this implies the desired result by the j=1j=1 case of Proposition  5.6 (a) and (c). ∎

Remark 5.10.

The gamma coefficients of the Narayana polynomials have a nice combinatorial interpretation in terms of lattice paths: (k−1)!(k−2​j+1)!​(j−1)!​j!\frac{(k-1)!}{(k-2j+1)!\,(j-1)!\,j!} is the number of Motzkin paths of length k−1k-1 with j−1j-1 up steps [3]. We can use this fact to give combinatorial interpretations of the gamma coefficients of W2​k+1,k​(t)W_{2k+1,k}(t) and W2​k−1,k​(t)W_{2k-1,k}(t). It would be interesting to find a combinatorial proof for Proposition  5.9 using Motzkin paths, perhaps in the vein of the “valley-hopping” proof for the γ\gamma-positivity of Narayana polynomials [5].

Our question in Remark 5.10 was recently been addressed by Fu and Yang [17], who gave a combinatorial proof for Proposition  5.9 using a group action, reminiscent of valley-hopping, on cyclic compositions.

While the polynomials Wn,k​(t)W_{n,k}(t) are not symmetric in general, it turns out that we can always express Wn,k​(t)W_{n,k}(t) as the sum of two symmetric polynomials.

Theorem 5.11.

Let 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n. Then there exist symmetric polynomials Wn,k+​(t)W_{n,k}^{+}(t) and Wn,k−​(t)W_{n,k}^{-}(t), both with nonnegative coefficients, such that:

  1. (a)

    if n<2​kn<2k, then Wn,k​(t)=Wn,k+​(t)−t​Wn,k−​(t)W_{n,k}(t)=W_{n,k}^{+}(t)-tW_{n,k}^{-}(t);

  2. (b)

    if n=2​kn=2k, then Wn,k​(t)=Wn,k+​(t)+t​Wn,k−​(t)W_{n,k}(t)=W_{n,k}^{+}(t)+tW_{n,k}^{-}(t);

  3. (c)

    and if n>2​kn>2k, then Wn,k​(t)=−Wn,k+​(t)+t​Wn,k−​(t)W_{n,k}(t)=-W_{n,k}^{+}(t)+tW_{n,k}^{-}(t).

Proof.

Since nn and kk are fixed, let us simplify notation by writing wmw_{m} in place of wn,k,mw_{n,k,m}, so that Wn,k​(t)=∑m=0kwm​tmW_{n,k}(t)=\sum_{m=0}^{k}w_{m}t^{m}. Let

(5.2) wi+1+=(∑j=0i+1wj)−(∑j=0iwk−j)andwi−=−(∑j=0iwj)+(∑j=0iwk−j)w^{+}_{i+1}=\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{i+1}w_{j}\Big)-\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{i}w_{k-j}\Big)\quad\text{and}\quad w^{-}_{i}=-\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{i}w_{j}\Big)+\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{i}w_{k-j}\Big)

for all 0≤i≤k0\leq i\leq k; also take w0+=1w^{+}_{0}=1 when k=nk=n and w0+=0w^{+}_{0}=0 otherwise. Observe that

(5.3) wi++wi−1−\displaystyle w^{+}_{i}+w^{-}_{i-1} =(∑j=0iwj)−(∑j=0i−1wk−j)−(∑j=0i−1wj)+(∑j=0i−1wk−j)=wi,\displaystyle=\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{i}w_{j}\Big)-\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}w_{k-j}\Big)-\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}w_{j}\Big)+\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}w_{k-j}\Big)=w_{i},
(5.4) wi+−wk−i+\displaystyle w^{+}_{i}-w^{+}_{k-i} =(∑j=0iwj)−(∑j=0i−1wk−j)−(∑j=0k−iwj)+(∑j=0k−i−1wk−j)=0,and\displaystyle=\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{i}w_{j}\Big)-\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}w_{k-j}\Big)-\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{k-i}w_{j}\Big)+\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{k-i-1}w_{k-j}\Big)=0,\quad\text{and}
(5.5) wi−1−−wk−i−\displaystyle w^{-}_{i-1}-w^{-}_{k-i} =−(∑j=0i−1wj)+(∑j=0i−1wk−j)+(∑j=0k−iwj)−(∑j=0k−iwk−j)=0.\displaystyle=-\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}w_{j}\Big)+\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}w_{k-j}\Big)+\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{k-i}w_{j}\Big)-\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{k-i}w_{k-j}\Big)=0.

A standard induction argument utilizing the explicit formula in Theorem  1.2 yields the following:

  • •

    the wi+w_{i}^{+} are positive when n≤2​kn\leq 2k,

  • •

    the wi+w_{i}^{+} are negative when n>2​kn>2k,

  • •

    the wi−w_{i}^{-} are positive when n≥2​kn\geq 2k, and

  • •

    the wi−w_{i}^{-} are negative when n<2​kn<2k.

Define the polynomials Wn,k+​(t)W_{n,k}^{+}(t) and Wn,k−​(t)W_{n,k}^{-}(t) by

Wn,k+​(t)=∑i=0k|wi+|​tiandWn,k−​(t)=∑i=0k|wi−|​ti,\displaystyle W_{n,k}^{+}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}|w_{i}^{+}|\,t^{i}\quad\text{and}\quad W_{n,k}^{-}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}|w_{i}^{-}|\,t^{i},

respectively. These polynomials are symmetric by (5.4) and (5.5), and the decompositions given in (a)–(c) hold by construction in light of (5.3). ∎

We end with a couple of conjectures concerning the polynomials Wn,k+​(t)W_{n,k}^{+}(t) and Wn,k−​(t)W_{n,k}^{-}(t) arising from our symmetric decomposition. Our first conjecture, concerning real-rootedness, has been numerically verified for all n≤100n\leq 100.

Conjecture 5.12.

The following completely characterizes when Wn,k+​(t)W_{n,k}^{+}(t) and Wn,k−​(t)W_{n,k}^{-}(t) are both real-rooted:

  1. (a)

    If n=1n=1 or n=2n=2, then Wn,k+​(t)W_{n,k}^{+}(t) and Wn,k−​(t)W_{n,k}^{-}(t) are both real-rooted if and only if k=1k=1.

  2. (b)

    If n>1n>1 and n≡1​ (mod 4)n\equiv 1\textup{ (mod 4)}, then Wn,k+​(t)W_{n,k}^{+}(t) and Wn,k−​(t)W_{n,k}^{-}(t) are both real-rooted if and only if k=1,2,⌊n/2⌋−1,⌊n/2⌋,or ⌊n/2⌋+1k=1,2,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor n/2}}\right\rfloor-1,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor n/2}}\right\rfloor,\text{or }\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor n/2}}\right\rfloor+1.

  3. (c)

    If n≡3​ (mod 4)n\equiv 3\textup{ (mod 4)}, then Wn,k+​(t)W_{n,k}^{+}(t) and Wn,k−​(t)W_{n,k}^{-}(t) are both real-rooted if and only if k=1,2,⌊n/2⌋−1,⌊n/2⌋,⌊n/2⌋+1,or ⌊n/2⌋+2k=1,2,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor n/2}}\right\rfloor-1,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor n/2}}\right\rfloor,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor n/2}}\right\rfloor+1,\text{or }\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\lfloor n/2}}\right\rfloor+2.

  4. (d)

    If nn is even and not equal to 22, 1010, 1212, or 1616, then Wn,k+​(t)W_{n,k}^{+}(t) and Wn,k−​(t)W_{n,k}^{-}(t) are both real-rooted if and only if k=1,2,n/2−1,n/2,or ​n/2+1k=1,2,n/2-1,n/2,\text{or }n/2+1.

  5. (e)

    If n=10n=10, 1212, or 1616, then Wn,k+​(t)W_{n,k}^{+}(t) and Wn,k−​(t)W_{n,k}^{-}(t) are both real-rooted if and only if k=1,2,n/2−2,n/2−1,n/2,or ​n/2+1k=1,2,n/2-2,n/2-1,n/2,\text{or }n/2+1.

To establish real-rootedness, it would be helpful to have formulas for the polynomials Wn,k+​(t)W_{n,k}^{+}(t) or Wn,k−​(t)W_{n,k}^{-}(t). Our next conjecture gives formulas for W2​k,k+​(t)W_{2k,k}^{+}(t), W2​k,k−​(t)W_{2k,k}^{-}(t), W2​k,k+1−​(t)W_{2k,k+1}^{-}(t), and W2​k,k−1+​(t)W_{2k,k-1}^{+}(t). Unfortunately, we do not have conjectured formulas for any of the other polynomials.

Conjecture 5.13.

Let k≥1k\geq 1.

  1. (a)

    We have

    W2​k,k+​(t)=(k−1)​Ck​Nark−1⁡(t)andW2​k,k−​(t)=Ck​∑i=0k−1OPEN(k−1iCLOSE)2​ti.W_{2k,k}^{+}(t)=(k-1)C_{k}\operatorname{Nar}_{k-1}(t)\quad\text{and}\quad W_{2k,k}^{-}(t)=C_{k}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\binom{k-1}{i}^{2}t^{i}.

    where Nar¯k(j)​(t)=∑i=0k−jj+1k+1​OPEN(k+1iCLOSE)​OPEN(k+1i+j+1CLOSE)​ti\overline{\operatorname{Nar}}_{k}^{(j)}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{k-j}\frac{j+1}{k+1}\binom{k+1}{i}\binom{k+1}{i+j+1}t^{i}.

6. Appendix

6.1. The generating function approach

Here we present an algebraic proof of Theorem 1.2, which gives an explicit formula for the numbers wn,k,mw_{n,k,m} and in turn implies the symmetry in Theorem 1.1. To do so, we need a functional equation satisfied by the generating function WW defined by

W=W⁡(x,y,z)=∑n,k,mwn,k,m​xn​yk​zm.W=W(x,y,z)=\sum_{n,k,m}w_{n,k,m}\,x^{n}y^{k}z^{m}.

In other words, WW is the generating function of all Dyck paths, where the exponents of xx, yy, and zz encode the semilength, the number of U​DUD-factors, and the number of U​U​DUUD-factors, respectively.

Lemma 6.1.

The functional equation

(6.1) (x−x2​y+x2​y​z)​W2−(1+x−x​y)​W+1=0(x-x^{2}y+x^{2}yz)W^{2}-(1+x-xy)W+1=0

holds.

Proof.

Let us call a Dyck path of positive semilength irreducible if it does not touch the horizontal axis, other than at its starting point and endpoint. Then each nonempty Dyck path PP uniquely decomposes as the concatenation of an irreducible Dyck path and a Dyck path (in that order), where the latter is the empty path if PP itself is irreducible. If V⁡(x,y,z)V(x,y,z) is the generating function for irreducible Dyck paths defined similarly to W⁡(x,y,z)W(x,y,z) but only for irreducible paths, then this leads to the functional equation

(6.2) W=1+V​W.W=1+VW.

Let II be an irreducible Dyck path; then II must start with an up step, end with a down step, and consist of a Dyck path P1P_{1} between the two. If P1P_{1} is empty, then II is simply the path U​DUD, contributing x​yxy to the generating function V⁡(x,y,z)V(x,y,z). Otherwise, I=U​P1​DI=UP_{1}D, and II has the same number of U​DUD-factors as P1P_{1}, while its semilength is one longer. The number of U​U​DUUD-factors of II compared with that of P1P_{1}, however, depends on whether P1P_{1} begins with a U​DUD, so let us consider these two cases separately:

  • •

    If P1P_{1} does begin with a U​DUD, then P1P_{1} is of the form U​D​P2UDP_{2} and I=U​P1​D=U​U​D​P2​DI=UP_{1}D=UUDP_{2}D has one more U​U​DUUD-factor than P1P_{1}. Therefore, in this case, II has one more U​DUD-factor and one more U​U​DUUD-factor than P2P_{2}, while its semilength is two longer. Dyck paths of this type contribute x2​y​z​Wx^{2}yzW to VV.

  • •

    If P1P_{1} does not begin with a U​DUD, then II also has the same number of U​U​DUUD-factors as P1P_{1}; Dyck paths of this type contribute x⁡(W−1−x​y​W)x(W-1-xyW) to the generating function VV.

Thus, we have the functional equation

(6.3) V=x​y+x2​y​z​W+x⁡(W−1−x​y​W).V=xy+x^{2}yzW+x(W-1-xyW).

The proof of our claim is now routine by substituting the expression obtained for VV in (6.3) into (6.2) and rearranging. ∎

Algebraic proof of Theorem  1.2.

Equation (6.1) can be rewritten as

u​W2−v​W+1=0,where ​u=x−x2​y+x2​y​z​ and ​v=1+x−x​y.uW^{2}-vW+1=0,\quad{\text{where }}u=x-x^{2}y+x^{2}yz{\text{ and }}v=1+x-xy.

Solving for WW in this second degree equation, after elementary manipulations, gives

OPENW=v−v2−4​u2​u=v2​u​(1−1−4​uv2CLOSE).W=\frac{v-\sqrt{v^{2}-4u}}{2u}=\frac{v}{2u}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1-\sqrt{1-4\frac{u}{v^{2}}}}}\right).

Setting t=u/v2t=u/v^{2} in the well known classical equation

1−1−4​t2​t=∑ν≥0Cν​tν,\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4t}}{2t}=\sum_{\nu\geq 0}C_{\nu}t^{\nu},

where Cν=OPEN(2​ννCLOSE)/(ν+1)C_{\nu}=\binom{2\nu}{\nu}/{(\nu+1)} is the νt​h\nu^{th} Catalan number, we expand WW as

(6.4) W=W⁡(x,y,z)=∑ν≥0Cν​(x−x2​y+x2​y​z)ν(1+x−x​y)2​ν+1,W=W(x,y,z)=\sum_{\nu\geq 0}C_{\nu}\,\frac{(x-x^{2}y+x^{2}yz)^{\nu}}{(1+x-xy)^{2\nu+1}},

whose terms are rational functions in xx, yy, and zz and there are no square roots involved. We now expand each term of (6.4) using a multinomial or negative binomial expansion. First, the multinomial expansion of the numerator takes the form

(6.5) (x−x2​y+x2​y​z)ν=∑i+j+m=νν!i!​j!​m!​xi​(−x2​y)j​(x2​y​z)m=∑i+j+m=ν(−1)j​ν!i!​j!​m!​xi+2​j+2​m​yj+m​zm.(x-x^{2}y+x^{2}yz)^{\nu}=\sum_{i+j+m=\nu}\frac{\nu!}{i!\,j!\,m!}x^{i}(-x^{2}y)^{j}(x^{2}yz)^{m}=\sum_{i+j+m=\nu}\frac{(-1)^{j}\nu!}{i!\,j!\,m!}x^{i+2j+2m}y^{j+m}z^{m}.

Next, the negative binomial expansion applied to the denominator gives

(6.6) (1+x−y​x)−(2​ν+1)=∑s(2​ν+s)!(2​ν)!​s!​(−x+y​x)s=∑ℓ,r(2​ν+ℓ+r)!(2​ν)!​ℓ!​r!​(−1)ℓ​yr​xℓ+r.(1+x-yx)^{-(2\nu+1)}=\sum_{s}\frac{(2\nu+s)!}{(2\nu)!\,s!}(-x+yx)^{s}=\sum_{\ell,r}\frac{(2\nu+\ell+r)!}{(2\nu)!\,\ell!\,r!}(-1)^{\ell}y^{r}x^{\ell+r}.

Then, multiplying (6.5) and (6.6), summing with respect to ν\nu, and taking into account that by (6.5) we have ν=i+j+m\nu=i+j+m, Equation (6.4) becomes

(6.7) W⁡(x,y,z)=∑i,j,m,ℓ,r(2​i+2​j+2​m+ℓ+r)!(i+j+m+1)!​i!​j!​m!​ℓ!​r!​(−1)j+ℓ​xi+2​j+2​m+ℓ+r​yj+m+r​zm.W(x,y,z)=\sum_{i,j,m,\ell,r}\frac{(2i+2j+2m+\ell+r)!}{(i+j+m+1)!\,i!\,j!\,m!\,\ell!\,r!}(-1)^{j+\ell}x^{i+2j+2m+\ell+r}y^{j+m+r}z^{m}.

Collecting terms in (6.7), we get

wn,k,m\displaystyle w_{n,k,m} =∑i+2​j+2​m+ℓ+r=nj+m+r=k(2​i+2​j+2​m+ℓ+r)!(i+j+m+1)!​i!​j!​m!​ℓ!​r!​(−1)j+ℓ\displaystyle=\!\!\!\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i+2j+2m+\ell+r=n\\ j+m+r=k\end{subarray}}\frac{(2i+2j+2m+\ell+r)!}{(i+j+m+1)!\,i!\,j!\,m!\,\ell!\,r!}(-1)^{j+\ell}
(6.8) =1m!​∑i+2​j+2​m+ℓ+r=nj+m+r=k(−1)j+ℓ​(2​i+2​j+2​m+ℓ+r)!(i+j+m+1)!​i!​j!​ℓ!​r!.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m!}\!\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i+2j+2m+\ell+r=n\\ j+m+r=k\end{subarray}}\frac{(-1)^{j+\ell}(2i+2j+2m+\ell+r)!}{(i+j+m+1)!\,i!\,j!\,\ell!\,r!}.

Now, solving the system {i+2j+2m+ℓ+r=n,j+m+r=k}\{i+2j+2m+\ell+r=n,j+m+r=k\} for ℓ,r≥0\ell,r\geq 0, the indexes ℓ\ell and rr must satisfy the conditions

(6.9) ℓ=n−k−m−i−j≥0andr=k−m−j≥0,\ell=n-k-m-i-j\geq 0\quad\text{and}\quad r=k-m-j\geq 0,

while i,j≥0i,j\geq 0. This implies that nn, kk, and mm must satisfy the inequalities

(6.10) m≤kandk+m≤nm\leq k\quad\text{and}\quad k+m\leq n

(otherwise the sum is empty and has value 00). Substituting in (6.8) the values of ℓ\ell and rr given by (6.9), the coefficient wn,k,mw_{n,k,m} is expressed as the double sum

(6.11) wn,k,m=1m!​∑i+j≤n−k−mj≤k−m(−1)n−k−m−i​(n+i)!(i+j+m+1)!​i!​j!​(n−k−m−i−j)!​(k−m−j)!.w_{n,k,m}=\frac{1}{m!}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i+j\leq n-k-m\\ j\leq k-m\end{subarray}}\frac{(-1)^{n-k-m-i}(n+i)!}{(i+j+m+1)!\,i!\,j!\,(n-k-m-i-j)!\,(k-m-j)!}.

This double sum can be greatly simplified using the Maple procedure “sum” as follows. Since the factorials in the denominators in (6.11) are ±∞\pm\infty when i,ji,j are big enough to be out of range, the corresponding terms in the double sum vanish. Hence, we can take the ranges i=0..infty and j=0..infty in the double sum. Typing the Maple command

> w[n,k,m] = 1/m!*sum(((-1)**(n-k-m-i)*(i+n)!/i!)*
sum(1/(i+j+m+1)!/j!/(n-i-j-k-m)!/(k-m-j)!,j=0..infinity),i=0..infinity);

produces the output

wn,k,m=−(−1CLOSE)n−k−mn!(m+1CLOSE)msin(π​k−π​nCLOSE)m!(m+1CLOSE)!(n−k−mCLOSE)!(k−mCLOSE)!sin(π​mCLOSE)(k−nCLOSE)(k−1−nCLOSE),w_{n,k,m}=-{\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(-1}}\right)^{n-k-m}n!\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m+1}}\right)m\,\sin\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\pi\,k-\pi\,n}}\right)}{m!\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m+1}}\right)!\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n-k-m}}\right)!\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-m}}\right)!\,\sin\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\pi\,m}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-n}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-1-n}}\right)}},

which we rewrite in the form

(6.12) wn,k,m=OPENOPEN(−1CLOSE)n−k−m​n!​(m+1CLOSE)m!(m+1CLOSE)!(n−k−mCLOSE)!(k−mCLOSE)!(n−k+1CLOSE)⋅q⁡(n,k,m)w_{n,k,m}={\frac{\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(-1}}\right)^{n-k-m}n!\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m+1}}\right)}{m!\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m+1}}\right)!\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n-k-m}}\right)!\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-m}}\right)!\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n-k+1}}\right)}}\cdot q(n,k,m)

where q⁡(n,k,m)q(n,k,m) takes the indeterminate form

q⁡(n,k,m)=m​sin⁡(π⁡(n−k))sin⁡(π​m)​(n−k)=00,q(n,k,m)=\frac{m\sin(\pi(n-k))}{\sin(\pi m)(n-k)}=\frac{0}{0},

since nn, kk, and mm are positive integers. We “lift” this indetermination by making use of the limits

(6.13) limt→0tsin⁡(π​t)\displaystyle\lim_{t\rightarrow 0}\frac{t}{\sin(\pi t)} =1πand\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\pi}\quad\text{and}
(6.14) limt→πsin⁡(k​t)sin⁡(ℓ​t)\displaystyle\lim_{t\rightarrow\pi}\frac{\sin(kt)}{\sin(\ell t)} =(−1)k−ℓ​kℓ,k∈ℤ,  0≠ℓ∈ℤ.\displaystyle=(-1)^{k-\ell}\,\frac{k}{\ell},\quad k\in\mathbb{Z},\,\,0\neq\ell\in\mathbb{Z}.

To complete the proof, we break into cases:

  • •

    If m=0m=0 and k=nk=n, then using (6.13) twice, we get q⁡(k,k,0)=1π⋅π1=1q(k,k,0)=\frac{1}{\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi}{1}=1. This implies, by (6.12), that wn,k,0=1w_{n,k,0}=1 when k=nk=n.

  • •

    If m=0m=0 and k≠nk\neq n, then by (6.10) we need only to consider the case k<nk<n. Hence, by (6.13) we get

    q⁡(n,k,0)=1π⋅sin⁡(π⁡(n−k))n−k=0,q(n,k,0)=\frac{1}{\pi}\cdot\frac{\sin(\pi(n-k))}{n-k}=0,

    since sin⁡(π⁡(n−k))=0\sin(\pi(n-k))=0 and n−k≠0n-k\neq 0. This implies that wk,0,n=0w_{k,0,n}=0 if k≠nk\neq n.

  • •

    If m>0m>0 and k+m≤nk+m\leq n, then we must have k<nk<n. Thus, by (6.14) with k=n−kk=n-k and ℓ=m\ell=m, we have

    q⁡(n,k,m)=mn−k⋅sin⁡(π⁡(n−k))sin⁡(π​m)=mn−k⋅(−1)n−k−m.q(n,k,m)=\frac{m}{n-k}\cdot\frac{\sin(\pi(n-k))}{\sin(\pi m)}=\frac{m}{n-k}\cdot(-1)^{n-k-m}.

    Substituting this value into (6.12) yields

    wn,k,m=n!m!(m−1CLOSE)!(n−k−mCLOSE)!(k−mCLOSE)!(n−kCLOSE)(n−k+1CLOSE),w_{n,k,m}={\frac{n!}{m!\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(m-1}}\right)!\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n-k-m}}\right)!\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(k-m}}\right)!\,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n-k}}\right)\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(n-k+1}}\right)}},

    which is equivalent to the desired expression in Theorem  1.2. ∎

In order to “cross check” our formula in Theorem 1.2, we computed the first terms of W⁡(x,y,z)W(x,y,z) using two methods: firstly, by making use of the explicit expression for the coefficients given in Theorem 1.2, and secondly, by making use of the Maple “mtaylor” command applied to (6.1). Both methods gave the same results displayed in Table 1.
